Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verses 1–7:

والمرسلت ........................................ لواقع

The real subject here is the occurrence of the Resurrection (qiyamah). The polytheists of Makkah found it hard to grasp how it would come about. The Qur'an addressed this matter in various styles and with various proofs and evidences. It was extremely necessary to place this question in the minds of these people, because without it the Islamic outlook on life could not settle in their minds, nor could the values of their lives be correctly determined, nor could the principles and branches of life be established. In all the heavenly scriptures and beliefs, the belief in the occurrence of the Resurrection has been the first step. In fact, the reform and correct construction of human life is not possible without it. The life of man and his deeds depend upon this belief. The various aspects of human life can be set right only through this belief, and correct conduct for man can be produced only through the concept of accountability on the Day of Resurrection. This is why the Qur'an made such a long and persistent effort to instill this belief in the minds of the Arabs, so that they might develop firm certainty in it.

At the beginning of the Surah, Allah swears an oath that the promise of the Hereafter is about to be fulfilled. The wording of the oath shows that the things by which Allah has sworn are also unseen realities. These are hidden forces, and in the system of this universe they are as effective as they are effective within human life. The early righteous scholars (salaf salihin) differed about the determination of their meaning. Some said that all these words refer to winds. Others said that they refer to angels. Still others said that some of the words refer to winds and some refer to angels. These varying interpretations show that their meaning and reference are, in any case, general and hidden. This vagueness, obscurity and lack of explicitness is more suitable to the reality over which the oath is being sworn, because it too is an unseen reality. Just as the things by which the oath is sworn, whether they are angels or winds, are effective in human life, so too the Resurrection will be effective in human life.

والمرسلت عرفا (77:1) "By those sent forth in succession." It is narrated from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that they refer to the angels. According to one narration from Masruq, Abu al-Duha and Mujahid, and likewise Al-Suddi, Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu Salih (according to one narration), the same report exists. In this case the meaning would be: by the angels who are sent successively with the commands of Allah, just as the mane of a horse is long and continuous. In a line, these angels come one after another. The same view has been expressed by them regarding 'asifat, nashirat, fariqat and mulqiyat, that they refer to angels.

It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that al-Mursalat 'urfa refers to winds. In this case the meaning would be that they move continuously and in succession, just as the manes of a horse move. The same opinion is held regarding their 'asifat and nashirat. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu Salih (according to one narration) also endorsed this.

Ibn Jarir refrained from deciding about al-Mursalat, saying that whether it refers to angels or winds only Allah knows. But regarding 'asifat he definitely took it to mean winds. The same view he expressed regarding nashirat, that they are the winds which scatter the clouds.

And it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that (al-fariqat farqa, al-mulqiyat dhikra, 'udhran aw nudhra) refers to angels. The same opinion is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, Mujahid, Qatadah, Rabi' ibn Anas, Al-Suddi and Al-Thawri. And there is no difference of opinion in this. These angels come to the Messengers with the commands of Allah and distinguish between truth and falsehood. They convey the revelation to the Messengers, and in it there is complete proof for people, whether as an excuse or as a warning.

My view is that the words, or their meaning, over which the oath is sworn have been deliberately kept undefined. For example, the meaning of (al-Dhariyat dharwa) and (al-Nazi'at gharqa) has been deliberately kept general. Moreover, the differences the earlier scholars have expressed regarding their meaning are also evidence that the meaning of these words, the thing sworn by, has been kept ambiguous, and that ambiguity at these places was itself the intended purpose. Therefore an allusive style is more appropriate at this place. These words, their vague indications, their continuity and rhythm, and the atmosphere they create, produce a vibration within human consciousness. This vibration and such stirring is more in harmony with the theme of this Surah and its direction. Every section of this Surah in fact gives a person a strong jolt and shakes him, calling him to give up these evil deeds and not to deny the manifest, outward and real signs of Allah. And if you do not give them up, then prepare yourself for the determined end of those who insist on denial.

ويل ............................ للمكذبين "Woe on that Day to those who deny."

After this, the human thought, outlook and consciousness are given a severe jolt: consider the day that will come, the day promised to all the Messengers, the day on which all the Messengers will present their performance, and the day on which the judgments of people's deeds will be made; how terrible that day will be.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verses 1–7:

والمرسلت ........................................ لواقع

The real subject here is the occurrence of the Resurrection (qiyamah). The polytheists of Makkah found it hard to grasp how it would come about. The Qur'an addressed this matter in various styles and with various proofs and evidences. It was extremely necessary to place this question in the minds of these people, because without it the Islamic outlook on life could not settle in their minds, nor could the values of their lives be correctly determined, nor could the principles and branches of life be established. In all the heavenly scriptures and beliefs, the belief in the occurrence of the Resurrection has been the first step. In fact, the reform and correct construction of human life is not possible without it. The life of man and his deeds depend upon this belief. The various aspects of human life can be set right only through this belief, and correct conduct for man can be produced only through the concept of accountability on the Day of Resurrection. This is why the Qur'an made such a long and persistent effort to instill this belief in the minds of the Arabs, so that they might develop firm certainty in it.

At the beginning of the Surah, Allah swears an oath that the promise of the Hereafter is about to be fulfilled. The wording of the oath shows that the things by which Allah has sworn are also unseen realities. These are hidden forces, and in the system of this universe they are as effective as they are effective within human life. The early righteous scholars (salaf salihin) differed about the determination of their meaning. Some said that all these words refer to winds. Others said that they refer to angels. Still others said that some of the words refer to winds and some refer to angels. These varying interpretations show that their meaning and reference are, in any case, general and hidden. This vagueness, obscurity and lack of explicitness is more suitable to the reality over which the oath is being sworn, because it too is an unseen reality. Just as the things by which the oath is sworn, whether they are angels or winds, are effective in human life, so too the Resurrection will be effective in human life.

والمرسلت عرفا (77:1) "By those sent forth in succession." It is narrated from Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) that they refer to the angels. According to one narration from Masruq, Abu al-Duha and Mujahid, and likewise Al-Suddi, Rabi' ibn Anas and Abu Salih (according to one narration), the same report exists. In this case the meaning would be: by the angels who are sent successively with the commands of Allah, just as the mane of a horse is long and continuous. In a line, these angels come one after another. The same view has been expressed by them regarding 'asifat, nashirat, fariqat and mulqiyat, that they refer to angels.

It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that al-Mursalat 'urfa refers to winds. In this case the meaning would be that they move continuously and in succession, just as the manes of a horse move. The same opinion is held regarding their 'asifat and nashirat. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu Salih (according to one narration) also endorsed this.

Ibn Jarir refrained from deciding about al-Mursalat, saying that whether it refers to angels or winds only Allah knows. But regarding 'asifat he definitely took it to mean winds. The same view he expressed regarding nashirat, that they are the winds which scatter the clouds.

And it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that (al-fariqat farqa, al-mulqiyat dhikra, 'udhran aw nudhra) refers to angels. The same opinion is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Masruq, Mujahid, Qatadah, Rabi' ibn Anas, Al-Suddi and Al-Thawri. And there is no difference of opinion in this. These angels come to the Messengers with the commands of Allah and distinguish between truth and falsehood. They convey the revelation to the Messengers, and in it there is complete proof for people, whether as an excuse or as a warning.

My view is that the words, or their meaning, over which the oath is sworn have been deliberately kept undefined. For example, the meaning of (al-Dhariyat dharwa) and (al-Nazi'at gharqa) has been deliberately kept general. Moreover, the differences the earlier scholars have expressed regarding their meaning are also evidence that the meaning of these words, the thing sworn by, has been kept ambiguous, and that ambiguity at these places was itself the intended purpose. Therefore an allusive style is more appropriate at this place. These words, their vague indications, their continuity and rhythm, and the atmosphere they create, produce a vibration within human consciousness. This vibration and such stirring is more in harmony with the theme of this Surah and its direction. Every section of this Surah in fact gives a person a strong jolt and shakes him, calling him to give up these evil deeds and not to deny the manifest, outward and real signs of Allah. And if you do not give them up, then prepare yourself for the determined end of those who insist on denial.

ويل ............................ للمكذبين "Woe on that Day to those who deny."

After this, the human thought, outlook and consciousness are given a severe jolt: consider the day that will come, the day promised to all the Messengers, the day on which all the Messengers will present their performance, and the day on which the judgments of people's deeds will be made; how terrible that day will be.

When the stars are dimmed and lose their light, and when the sky is split open, and when the mountains are blown away like wisps of cotton. Such scenes and sights are described in various surahs of the Quran in different ways. The summary of them all is that on the Day of Resurrection this visible universe will no longer remain as it is, and its fabric will be rolled up. These celestial spheres will be shattered into pieces. There will be tremendous explosions, and these great explosions will be of the same kind as the explosions that people see on a small scale in the form of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. It is as if on the Day of Resurrection these earthquakes, explosions and volcanic events will occur on a very vast scale, like the firecrackers that children set off on the occasion of Eid and Shab-e-Qadr, or like atomic explosions and hydrogen explosions. But the horrors produced by the collision of the spheres of the whole universe with one another will be far greater. They are beyond human imagination, and after these explosions it will be impossible for human beings to remain alive and watch the spectacle.

After these explosions and horrors, the surah then tells us that another great event will take place, namely that the Messengers will be told to present their report on the performance of their duty of prophethood. The time will come for the appearance of the Messengers, from Adam (peace be upon him) to Muhammad (ﷺ). This reckoning will be so great that for it the whole universe will be shaken by an earthquake to prepare the ground. All the decisions of earthly life will then be made, and every decision will be under the commands of Allah. And the final judgment on the end of all generations will be pronounced.

The Quran has presented this matter in an extremely terrifying manner, from which it becomes clear that this is a very great reality, so great that a human being cannot fully comprehend it.

And when the Messengers are brought to their appointed time. For what day has it been postponed? For the Day of Decision. And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?

This manner of expression itself shows that a great matter is being spoken of. When terror and dread have settled upon the screen of human consciousness, since the Messengers have been summoned to account, the stars have lost their light, and the mountains have flown away like tufts of wool, then in this state of fear and dread, there comes this further terror.

Woe on that Day to those who deny. ﴿Woe on that Day to those who deny﴾ (77:15).

This warning comes from Allah, the Mighty (ʿAzīz), the Compeller (Jabbār), and it follows the conditions that will be imposed upon this universe. The Messengers will be brought forward, and they too will be called to account for their performance, and each of them will present his account one by one. In such circumstances this warning is certainly extremely effective, and a sensitive soul is indeed overcome with fear to the point of fainting.

Now, drawing the human being away from the terrors of the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Faṣl) and the Day of Reckoning (Yawm al-Ḥisāb), the passage brings him back to the human history of this very world, so that the bewildered human being may reflect a little upon his own history.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verses 16–17:

Alam nuhlik ........................ lil-mukadhdhibin

Thus, in a single stroke, a glimpse is shown of the destructions of the earlier nations and peoples, and then a glimpse is shown of those who came after them. Yet in both distant and recent history, examples of destroyed nations are countless. As far as the eye can see, across both distant and near eras, all that appears are the corpses of nations, and through the tongue of circumstance, the echo of God's sunnah is seen and heard.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verses 16–17:

Alam nuhlik ........................ lil-mukadhdhibin

Thus do We deal with the criminals. (77:18) That is the enduring way of Allah. It never ceases, and never changes its course. When the criminals come to know that their end will be like that of the criminals of earlier times and of those nearer to them, then a curse of destruction comes upon them, and a curse from Allah is a decree of destruction.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verse 19:

﴿Woe on that Day to those who deny.﴾ (77:19)

Now our journey takes another turn: away from the sight of destruction, ruin and corpses, toward a journey of creation and construction, of how Allah's system of creation, His system of lordship (rububiyyah) and His system of governance (tadbir) operates.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Qur'an, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verses 20–22:

﴿Did We not create you...﴾ ... ﴿...woe that Day to the deniers﴾

This refers to the long and wondrous journey of the embryo in the womb. The Qur'an describes this lengthy organic process in a few vivid glimpses: a humble drop of water, then its placement in a secure and protected place of settlement, for a determined period, within a clear system and measure, and the comment on that system and measure.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verse 24:

Woe (Wayl) ... to the deniers on that Day (24:77): "Woe on that Day to those who denied."

After this, the study journey of this earth: this journey concerns human life, and the establishment of all the necessities for this life within the earth, and its study.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verses 25–28:

Did We not make the earth a receptacle, holding both the living and the dead? And We set in it lofty mountains, and We gave you sweet water to drink. Woe that day to the deniers!

That is, We have made the earth such that it gathers within its embrace both living and dead things, and We have fixed within it towering, lofty mountains that stand firm and high. Upon them clouds hover at all times, and from them sweet water flows. All of this is a manifestation of Allah's great power and of precisely measured proportions, and it points to profound wisdom. Therefore the deniers have no justification for denying.

Now, after presenting these signs of power and the profound, wise laws of nature, and after filling human consciousness with impressions and feelings, the direction of discourse turns to reckoning and the Day of Recompense. We hear a most awe-inspiring command, in which the deniers are told: "Rise up and set off toward the punishment that you used to deny." This command is delivered in a manner of extreme rebuke and distress.

That is, "Go, now you are free; the decisions of the long day of Resurrection have now been made. But this freedom is now a permanent imprisonment, inside Hell."

﴿Go forward to that which you used to deny.﴾ (77:29) This thing is now present before you. What is it?

"Proceed to the shadow with three branches, (30) (77:30)" — the passage quoted here is Qur'anic text, so the translation of the verse is: "Go towards that which you used to deny. Go towards a shadow with three branches."

Let me be precise and render the passage as it stands:

Go on to the shadow having three branches, [the verse reads:] "Proceed to a shadow of three branches." This is the smoke of Hell, whose branches have spread further, extending into three parts. However, this is nonetheless better than a flame of fire, but

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 77, verse 31:

﴿Neither cooling nor protecting from the flame of the fire.﴾ This appears to be shade, but in it there is suffocation; it is intensely hot and like the flame of fire. The word "shade" is said here merely as mockery. Rather, in this way a longing is created in their hearts that, if only there were some shade in which they could take refuge.

Come, but you know where you have to go now, and in the light of the decision that has been made you know your destination, so there is no need for explanation and elaboration. And see what "it" is doing wherever you go.

Verse 32–33 (Qur'an 77:32–33): "Indeed, it throws sparks like palaces, as if they were yellow camels."

Sparks will fly out like great palaces of stone, as if they were huge stones piling up on one another and falling. (The Arabs used the word qusur (palaces) for houses built of stone. It is not necessary that the intended meaning be the enormous palaces of today.) And these sparks will go forward and backward like yellow camels. These are the sparks of that fire. Now, what that fire will be like—may Allah protect us from it. In this frightful condition, a repeated remark is being made.

Woe on that Day to those who deny.

These people will be in shade, and this is real shade, not the shade of smoke, which has three branches. It is neither cool nor does it protect from the flames of fire. These people will be among springs, not in smoke that chokes the throat.

"And fruits of whatever they desire" (77:42-43). "Fruits of what they desire." Besides these material rewards and comforts, they will also be given a spiritual reward: they will be called out before all the witnesses, with the greatest honour.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verses 43–44:

﴿Kulū wa-ishrabū﴾ ... ﴿al-muḥsinīn﴾ (44:77) "Eat and drink with enjoyment, as a reward for what you used to do. Thus do We reward the good-doers."

This is a great honour: a royal notification will be issued concerning them. And the final comment.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 77, verses 43–44:

﴿Kulū wa-ishrabū﴾ ... ﴿al-muḥsinīn﴾ (44:77) "Eat and drink with enjoyment, as a reward for what you used to do. Thus do We reward the good-doers."

This is a great honour: a royal notification will be issued concerning them. And the final comment.

"Woe on that Day to those who deny!" (77:45) — "Woe" is the verdict on those who deny, and this remark stands in contrast to the blessings mentioned before it.

Here the context is no longer a passing allusion but a glimpse. It is a glimpse of the affairs of this worldly life, which on the Day of Resurrection are now rolled up. We see once more its picture and a glimpse of it on the screen, in which the humiliation and disgrace of those who denied are displayed.

It is as though we are watching a film of the world within the field of the Hereafter, and this glimpse is shown to us in just two sentences. It is as though we are seeing these glimpses with our own eyes. Although the periods of this world and the Hereafter are long, in the Hereafter this address is to the muttaqun (the God-conscious), whereas in this world it is addressed to the mujrimun (the guilty), and through the language of circumstance it is being said: behold how great the difference will be between the conditions of the two, namely that one group is eating and drinking abundantly during this brief span, and will then be deprived for long ages.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 77, verse 47:

"Woe on that Day to those who deny" (77:47). "Today, in the Day of Resurrection, there is destruction for those who deny." And after the Resurrection, times will not come to an end.

Now astonishment is being expressed at the addressees of the Qur'an, that such a call is being given to them and yet they do not accept it.

Yet they are looking on, and they are being explained and warned in such an eloquent manner. If they are not affected by this style of speech, by which mountains are moved and an earthquake comes upon even inanimate things, then after this no speech will be effective upon them. It is as though these people are extremely wretched, ill-fated, and destined for a bad end. Destruction is written in their fate, and gentle and delicate speech has no effect upon them.

This entire surah, because of its subjects, its manner of expression, the melody of its words, its frightening scenes and tableaux, and its piercing, sharp indications, is so impactful that no heart can stand its ground against it. No existence can remain unaffected by it. Even the hardest heart melts. But if even this surah has no effect upon these people, then may their Lord be their only protector!

Glory be to Allah, what a speech this Qur'an is! How firm is its grip. How much power there is in it!!
